q1: SELECT ITM.ITEMN, ITPV.VENDN FROM ITM ITM, (SELECT DISTINCT ITP.ITEMN, PUR.VENDN FROM ITP ITP, PUR PUR WHERE ITP.PONUM = PUR.PONUM AND PUR.ODATE > 85) ITPV WHERE ITM.ITEMN = ITPV.ITEMN AND ITM.ITEMN > 1 AND ITM.ITEMN < 20
q2: SELECT DISTINCT ITM.ITEMN, PUR.VENDN FROM ITM ITM, ITP ITP, PUR PUR WHERE ITP.PONUM = PUR.PONUM AND ITM.ITEMN = ITP.ITEMN AND PUR.ODATE > 85 AND ITM.ITEMN > 1 AND ITM.ITEMN < 20
explanation: After analysing the two statements it turns out they are already relational-set equivalent: both ultimately return the set of (ITEMN , VENDN) pairs that (1) come from some purchase whose ODATE > 85 and (2) have an ITEMN that exists in ITM with 1 < ITEMN < 20.  The extra DISTINCT that appears either in the sub-query (Q1) or at the top level (Q2) only removes duplicate (ITEMN,VENDN) pairs; because ITM.ITEMN is a primary key, no additional duplicates can be (re-)introduced by the final join in Q1.  Consequently, for every possible database that respects the given constraints, Q1 and Q2 always return exactly the same rows.
counterexample_dsp: None – the queries are equivalent, so no data set can make them differ.

q1: SELECT Z.A, Z.B FROM R1 X, R2 Y, R2 Z WHERE X.A = Y.A AND Y.A = Z.A AND X.A = Z.A AND Y.B = Z.B
q2: SELECT Z.A, Z.B FROM R1 X, R2 Y, R2 Z WHERE X.A = Y.A AND Y.A = Z.A AND X.A = Z.A
explanation: The two queries are identical except that Q1 adds the extra filter  "Y.B = Z.B".  Because R2’s primary-key is only on column A, there is at most one R2 row for any given A, so normally Y.B and Z.B come from the same row and would be equal.  However SQL’s three-valued logic makes the equality test evaluate to UNKNOWN (and therefore fail) whenever either side is NULL.  Q2 has no such test, so rows whose R2.B is NULL are kept by Q2 but rejected by Q1; hence the result sets can differ whenever an R2 row participating in the join contains a NULL in column B.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO R1 (A, B) VALUES (1, 100);
INSERT INTO R2 (A, B) VALUES (1, NULL);
counterexample_dsp: Put one R1 row and one matching R2 row that shares the same A value, but let that R2 row have B = NULL.  Because NULL = NULL is UNKNOWN, the extra predicate in Q1 filters the row out, while Q2 still returns it.  No schema constraints are violated because column B is nullable and the primary-key constraint on (A) is respected.

q1: SELECT ITEMPRICE.NP, ITM.TYPE, ITM.ITEMNO FROM (SELECT DISTINCT ITP.ITEMNO AS ITN, ITP.NP AS NP FROM ITP ITP WHERE ITP.NP > 1000) ITEMPRICE, ITM ITM WHERE ITEMPRICE.ITN = ITM.ITEMNO
q2: SELECT DISTINCT ITP.NP, ITM.TYPE, ITM.ITEMNO FROM ITP ITP, ITM ITM WHERE ITP.NP > 1000 AND ITP.ITEMNO = ITM.ITEMNO
explanation: Q1 first removes duplicate (ITEMNO , NP) pairs that satisfy NP > 1000 and only afterwards joins the resulting set with ITM.  Q2 first joins every qualifying ITP row with ITM and then removes duplicates on the (NP , TYPE , ITEMNO) combination.  Because (a) ITM contains at most one row per ITEMNO (PRIMARY KEY), and (b) the DISTINCT in Q2 is applied on the same three attributes that appear in the final projection of Q1, the two queries always produce exactly the same set of result rows.  Any duplicate elimination that happens in Q1’s inner sub-query would also happen – possibly a little later – in Q2’s outer DISTINCT.  Hence the queries are equivalent under the given schema.
counterexample_dsp: No data configuration can make the two queries return different results; therefore a counterexample does not exist for the supplied schema and queries.

q1: SELECT ITM.ITEMNO, ITEMPRICE.NP FROM (SELECT DISTINCT ITP.ITEMNO AS ITN, ITP.NP AS NP FROM ITP ITP) ITEMPRICE, ITM ITM WHERE ITEMPRICE.ITN = ITM.ITEMNO
q2: SELECT DISTINCT ITM.ITEMNO, ITP.NP FROM ITP ITP, ITM ITM WHERE ITP.ITEMNO = ITM.ITEMNO
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are actually equivalent.  Both return the set of distinct (ITEMNO, NP) pairs that occur in ITP and whose ITEMNO also appears in ITM.  In Q1 the DISTINCT is applied inside a sub-query before the join; in Q2 the DISTINCT is applied after the join.  Because ITM has at most one row per ITEMNO (primary key) the place where the DISTINCT is applied cannot change which (ITEMNO, NP) pairs survive – it only changes how many duplicates are discarded.  Therefore no database instance can make the two queries return different results.
counterexample_dsp: No counterexample is possible; the queries are equivalent for all databases that satisfy the given schema and constraints.

q1: SELECT * FROM ITP ITP WHERE ITP.ITEMN IN (SELECT ITL.ITEMN FROM ITL ITL WHERE ITL.WKCEN = 468 AND ITL.LOCAN = 0)
q2: SELECT DISTINCT ITP.* FROM ITP ITP, ITL ITL WHERE ITP.ITEMN = ITL.ITEMN AND ITL.WKCEN = 468 AND ITL.LOCAN = 0
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are in fact equivalent for every possible database that satisfies the given schema.  Both queries simply return all rows of ITP whose ITEMN occurs in at least one ITL row with (WKCEN = 468 AND LOCAN = 0).  Q2 does the same thing through an inner–join and then removes potential duplicates with DISTINCT; however, because ITP’s primary-key is (ITEMN), duplicates of ITP.* cannot occur in the final projection, so DISTINCT never changes the result.  No construct (NULL handling, duplicate elimination, missing matches, etc.) can make the two queries diverge under the stated schema constraints, therefore a counterexample does not exist.
counterexample_dsp: Impossible – there is no data configuration that makes the result sets differ.

q1: SELECT T.TMEMBER FROM DEPTS D, TEAMS T WHERE D.DPROJ = T.TPROJ AND D.DNAME = 'SECURITY'
q2: SELECT V1.E FROM (SELECT D.DNAME AS D, D.DPROJ AS P, P.EMPL AS E FROM DEPTS D, PAYROLL P WHERE D.DNAME = P.PDEPT) V1, (SELECT T.TMEMBER AS E, P.PDEPT AS D, T.TPROJ AS P FROM TEAMS T, PAYROLL P WHERE T.TMEMBER = P.EMPL) V2 WHERE V1.D = 'SECURITY' AND V1.P = V2.P AND V1.E = V2.E AND V1.D = V2.D
explanation: Q1 only checks that a SECURITY department (DNAME = 'SECURITY') shares a project with a team member, so every team-member that works on that project is returned.  Q2 does a lot more: besides the same project match it also requires that the employee’s payroll record (PAYROLL.PDEPT) equals the department name SECURITY.  Therefore an employee whose team project belongs to the SECURITY department but whose payroll department is something else will be returned by Q1 but filtered out by Q2.
counterexample_dsp: Make one SECURITY department (project 1).  Put one employee (id 10) in that project through TEAMS, but let his payroll department be a DIFFERENT value.  The foreign-key from TEAMS to PAYROLL is satisfied, yet Q2 rejects the row because PAYROLL.PDEPT <> 'SECURITY', while Q1 keeps it.

q1: SELECT Y.* FROM PAYROLL X, APPLICANT Y WHERE X.SSNO = Y.SSNO AND X.DEPTNO = 29
q2: SELECT C.* FROM PAYROLL A, (SELECT Y.SSNO, Y.DEPTNO FROM PAYROLL Y) B, APPLICANT C WHERE A.SSNO = B.SSNO AND C.SSNO = A.SSNO AND B.DEPTNO = 29
schema:
CREATE TABLE PAYROLL (SSNO INT, DEPTNO INT);
CREATE TABLE APPLICANT (SSNO INT, JOBTITILE INT, OFFICENO INT);
explanation: Both queries want applicants whose SSNO appears in PAYROLL with DEPTNO = 29.   Q1 joins APPLICANT with only the payroll rows that already satisfy DEPTNO = 29, so every qualifying applicant will appear exactly as many times as there are DEPTNO-29 payroll rows.   Q2 first builds a self-join of PAYROLL (aliases A and B).  It keeps every pair where the two rows share the same SSNO and the B-side row has DEPTNO = 29.  Because A is **not** filtered on DEPTNO, any additional payroll rows (different DEPTNOs but same SSNO) multiply the result.  Therefore Q2 can return more duplicates than Q1 whenever an SSNO owns at least one DEPTNO = 29 row **and** at least one other row with a different department.
counterexample_dsp: Create one SSNO that has two payroll records – one in department 29 and one in another department.  Give that SSNO exactly one applicant row.  Q1 will output the applicant once (only the DEPTNO = 29 payroll row matches), while Q2 will output the applicant twice (the DEPTNO = 29 B-row pairs with both payroll rows on the A-side).

q1: SELECT X.NAME AS XN FROM EMP X WHERE (X.EMP, X.DEPT) IN (SELECT Y.MGR, Y.DEPT FROM DEPT Y WHERE Y.LOC = 3)
q2: SELECT X.NAME AS XN FROM EMP X, DEPT Y WHERE X.DEPT = Y.DEPT AND Y.LOC = 3 AND X.EMP = Y.MGR
schema:
CREATE TABLE EMP (NAME INT, DEPT INT, EMP INT);
CREATE TABLE DEPT (DEPT INT, LOC INT, MGR INT);
explanation: Q1 only checks whether a (EMP , DEPT) pair exists in DEPT for LOC = 3.  It returns each qualifying employee once, because the IN-predicate is just a Boolean filter.  Q2 materialises a join between EMP and every matching DEPT row.  If the same (MGR , DEPT , LOC) row occurs several times in DEPT, the join produces one result row per copy, while Q1 still produces only one.  Hence duplicate rows in DEPT make the two queries return different multisets of rows.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO EMP  (NAME, DEPT, EMP) VALUES
  (1, 10, 100);

INSERT INTO DEPT (DEPT, LOC, MGR) VALUES
  (10, 3, 100),  -- duplicate 1, causes second copy in join
  (10, 3, 100),  -- duplicate 2
  (10, 2, 100);  -- different LOC, ignored by both queries
counterexample_dsp: Put one employee (NAME = 1, EMP = 100, DEPT = 10).  Insert two identical DEPT rows (DEPT = 10, LOC = 3, MGR = 100) plus one irrelevant row.  For this data Q1 returns the employee once, Q2 returns the same employee twice because it joins with both duplicate DEPT rows.

q1: SELECT X.B AS XB FROM R X WHERE X.A = 5 AND X.C < 1
q2: SELECT X.B AS XB FROM R X WHERE X.A < 10
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A INT, B INT, C INT);
explanation: Q1 only returns column B from rows where A = 5 AND C < 1.  Q2 returns column B from any row where A < 10 (no condition on C).  Therefore every row that satisfies Q1 will also satisfy Q2, but any row with A < 10 that either has A ≠ 5 or has A = 5 with C ≥ 1 appears only in Q2, making the two result sets different.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO R (A, B, C) VALUES
  (5,  10, 0),   -- returned by both Q1 and Q2
  (3,  20, 0);   -- returned only by Q2
counterexample_dsp: Create one tuple that satisfies both queries (A = 5, C < 1) and one tuple that satisfies only Q2 (A < 10 but A ≠ 5).  The second tuple causes Q2 to return an extra B-value that Q1 does not return, proving the queries are not equivalent.

q1:
SELECT 
    P.UID,
    P.UNAME,
    COALESCE(Q.CNT, 0) AS CNT
FROM (
    SELECT X.UID, X.UNAME
    FROM USER X
    WHERE X.CITY = 3
) AS P
LEFT JOIN (
    SELECT Y.UID, COUNT(*) AS CNT
    FROM PICTURE Y
    WHERE Y.SIZE > 1000000
    GROUP BY Y.UID
) AS Q
USING (UID);
q2: SELECT X.UID AS UID, X.UNAME AS UNAME, COUNT(*) AS CNT FROM USER X, PICTURE Y WHERE X.UID = Y.UID AND Y.SIZE > 1000000 AND X.CITY = 3 GROUP BY X.UID, X.UNAME
schema:
CREATE TABLE USER (UID INT, UNAME INT, CITY INT);
CREATE TABLE PICTURE (UID INT, SIZE INT);
explanation:
Q1 keeps ALL users that live in CITY = 3 because it first filters the USER table, then LEFT-JOINs the result with the large-picture counts.  Users that have no picture larger than 1 000 000 still appear with CNT = 0 (thanks to the outer join and COALESCE).
Q2, in contrast, uses an INNER join between USER and PICTURE while simultaneously enforcing the size and city predicates.  Therefore only those CITY = 3 users that actually own at least one picture larger than 1 000 000 are returned.  The outer-vs-inner join choice is the single reason the two queries can return different result sets.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO USER (UID, UNAME, CITY) VALUES
  (1, 101, 3),  -- user in city 3, no large picture
  (2, 102, 3);  -- user in city 3, has a large picture

INSERT INTO PICTURE (UID, SIZE) VALUES
  (1, 500000),   -- small picture, not counted
  (2, 1500000);  -- large picture to be counted
counterexample_dsp: Provide one user located in CITY = 3 who owns NO qualifying (SIZE > 1 000 000) pictures.  Q1 will show this user with CNT = 0, whereas Q2 will not return the user at all.  A second user with at least one large picture is added to show that counts agree when a match exists.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT X.USRUID AS XID, X.USRNAME AS XNAME FROM USR X, PIC U, PIC V, PIC W WHERE X.USRUID = U.PICUID AND X.USRUID = V.PICUID AND X.USRUID = W.PICUID AND W.PICSIZE = V.PICSIZE AND U.PICSIZE < 500000 and V.PICSIZE >= 500000
q2: SELECT DISTINCT X.USRUID AS XID, X.USRNAME AS XNAME FROM USR X, PIC U, PIC V WHERE X.USRUID = U.PICUID AND X.USRUID = V.PICUID AND U.PICSIZE < 500000 and V.PICSIZE >= 500000
schema:
CREATE TABLE USR (USRUID INT, USRNAME VARCHAR);
CREATE TABLE PIC (PICUID INT, PICSIZE INT);
explanation: No counter-example exists: every (X,U,V) pair that satisfies Q2 can always be extended to an (X,U,V,W) quadruple that satisfies Q1 by simply re-using the same row chosen for V as W (its PICSIZE is of course equal to itself). Conversely, any result produced by Q1 already satisfies the conditions of Q2. Therefore Q1 ≡ Q2 for every possible database state.
counterexample_dsp: Impossible – the two queries are semantically equivalent, so there is no data that can make their result sets differ.

q1: SELECT X.PNUM AS XP FROM PARTS X WHERE (X.PNUM, X.QOH) IN (SELECT Y.PNUM, COUNT(Y.SHIPDATE) AS CNT FROM SUPPLY Y WHERE Y.SHIPDATE < 10)
q2: SELECT X.PNUM AS XP FROM PARTS X, (SELECT Y.PNUM AS SUPPNUM, COUNT(Y.SHIPDATE) AS CT FROM SUPPLY Y WHERE Y.SHIPDATE < 10 GROUP BY Y.PNUM) TEMP WHERE X.QOH = TEMP.CT AND X.PNUM = TEMP.SUPPNUM
schema:
CREATE TABLE PARTS (PNUM INT, QOH INT);
CREATE TABLE SUPPLY (PNUM INT, SHIPDATE INT);
explanation:
Q1 compares each row in PARTS with ONE single pair (PNUM , CNT) coming from the sub-query. Because the sub-query contains an aggregate (COUNT) but NO GROUP BY, most engines (e.g. MySQL with ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY off) treat it as “aggregate over the whole table”, returning exactly one row that holds the global count together with an arbitrary PNUM value.  
Q2 first groups SUPPLY by PNUM, producing one (PNUM , CNT) pair per part number and then joins that result set with PARTS.  
Hence Q1 can match at most one part (the one whose (PNUM , QOH) happens to equal the single pair coming from the sub-query), while Q2 may match many parts – one for every PNUM whose local count equals its QOH.  Whenever SUPPLY contains at least two different PNUM values, the two queries can return different answer sets.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO PARTS (PNUM, QOH) VALUES
  (1, 3),   -- Q1 will pick this one (global count = 3)
  (1, 2),   -- Q2 will pick this one (local count for PNUM 1 = 2)
  (2, 1);   -- Q2 will also pick this one (local count for PNUM 2 = 1)

INSERT INTO SUPPLY (PNUM, SHIPDATE) VALUES
  (1, 5),   -- <10
  (1, 6),   -- <10  -> local count for PNUM 1 = 2
  (2, 2);   -- <10  -> local count for PNUM 2 = 1, global count = 3
counterexample_dsp: Create two different PNUMs in SUPPLY that have shipdate<10 so Q2 will produce two different counts.  Insert PARTS rows whose QOH equals the per-PNUM counts (to be returned by Q2) plus one extra PARTS row whose QOH equals the GLOBAL count (to be returned by Q1).  This makes Q1 return only one PNUM, while Q2 returns two.

q1: SELECT X.NAME AS XN FROM EMP X WHERE (X.EMP, X.DEPT) IN (SELECT Y.MGR, Y.DEPT FROM DEPT Y WHERE Y.LOC = 3)
q2: SELECT X.NAME AS XN FROM EMP X
schema:
CREATE TABLE EMP (NAME INT, DEPT INT, EMP INT);
CREATE TABLE DEPT (DEPT INT, LOC INT, MGR INT);
explanation: Q2 simply lists every NAME that exists in EMP, while Q1 first demands that the tuple (EMP,DEPT) of that row also occurs among those DEPT-rows whose LOC = 3.  Therefore any EMP row whose (EMP,DEPT) pair is missing from the DEPT table at LOC 3 will appear in Q2 but be filtered out of Q1, so the queries are not equivalent.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO EMP  (NAME, DEPT, EMP)  VALUES (1, 10, 100);
INSERT INTO DEPT (DEPT, LOC,  MGR) VALUES (10,  2, 100);
counterexample_dsp: Add one EMP row whose (EMP,DEPT) combination is **not** present in any DEPT row with LOC = 3 (it can be absent altogether, or present only with a different LOC value).  That row passes Q2 but fails Q1, producing different outputs.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT X.X AS AX FROM A X, B Y WHERE X.YA = Y.YB
q2:
SELECT X.X AS AX
FROM A X, A Y, B Z
WHERE X.X = Y.X
  AND X.YA = Z.YB

UNION ALL

SELECT 1 AS AX
FROM A X
WHERE 1 = 0;
schema:
CREATE TABLE A (X INT, YA INT);
CREATE TABLE B (YB INT);
explanation: Q1 keeps only unique A.X values that find a matching B.YB (because of DISTINCT), while Q2 keeps every matching combination of rows coming from A-as-X, A-as-Y and B (it has no DISTINCT). As soon as more than one join combination produces the same X value – e.g. because B contains two equal YB rows – Q2 will output that value several times, whereas Q1 will output it once. Therefore the two queries are not equivalent under multiset (bag) semantics.
counterexample_dsp: Make A contain one row (X=10, YA=100) and make B contain two rows with the same value YB=100. The single A row joins with both B rows, producing two identical AX=10 rows in Q2, but only one AX=10 row in Q1 due to DISTINCT.

q1: SELECT X.X AS AX FROM A X WHERE X.YX = 'HELLO'
q2: SELECT X.X AS AX FROM A X WHERE X.YX = 'HELLO HI'
schema: CREATE TABLE A (X INT, YA INT, YX VARCHAR);
explanation: Q1 returns the X values of rows whose YX column is exactly the string 'HELLO', while Q2 returns the X values of rows whose YX column is exactly the string 'HELLO HI'. Because each query compares YX to a different literal, they will differ whenever at least one row matches just one of those two literals.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO A (X, YA, YX) VALUES (1, 100, 'HELLO');
INSERT INTO A (X, YA, YX) VALUES (2, 200, 'HELLO HI');
counterexample_dsp: Insert one row where YX = 'HELLO' and a different row where YX = 'HELLO HI'. Q1 will output the X of the first row; Q2 will output the X of the second row, making the result sets different.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT X.X AS X FROM R1 X, R2 Y WHERE X.Y = Y.Y AND X.X = 1
q2: SELECT DISTINCT X.X AS X FROM R1 X, R1 Y, R2 Z WHERE X.X = Y.X AND X.Y = Z.Y AND X.X = 1
schema:
CREATE TABLE R1 (X INT, Y INT);
CREATE TABLE R2 (Y INT);
explanation: Q1 returns the value 1 if (and only if) there is at least one row in R1 with X = 1 whose Y-value also appears in R2.  Q2 imposes the very same requirement: it chooses some row X from R1 with X = 1, finds *any* (possibly the same) row Y in R1 that also has X = 1, and finally requires a row Z in R2 with Z.Y = X.Y.  Because the extra self-join “X.X = Y.X” never filters the row X out (X itself already satisfies it), Q2 succeeds in exactly the same situations in which Q1 succeeds.  Hence the result sets of the two queries are identical for every possible database state; no data configuration can make them diverge.
counterexample: -- (no INSERT statements – the queries are provably equivalent)
counterexample_dsp: Not applicable – the queries are equivalent; therefore a counterexample database instance does not exist.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT * FROM R X WHERE X.A1 = X.A2 AND X.A2 = X.A3
q2: SELECT DISTINCT * FROM R X WHERE X.A1 = X.A2 AND X.A1 = X.A3
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A1 INT, A2 INT, A3 INT);
explanation: The two WHERE-clauses are logically identical for every possible row of table R.  In order for a row to satisfy Q1 the predicates (A1 = A2) AND (A2 = A3) must both evaluate to TRUE.  If they are both TRUE then all three column values are equal and non-NULL.  The same is required by Q2, whose predicates are (A1 = A2) AND (A1 = A3).  Because equality is symmetric and, for non-NULL values, transitive, the second predicate list is satisfied by exactly the same rows as the first.  Columns are of type INT (so no collation or floating-point anomalies can break transitivity), and NULL handling is identical in both queries (any NULL makes one of the predicates UNKNOWN, causing the whole AND expression to be FALSE).  Consequently, for every possible state of R the two SELECT DISTINCT statements return the very same set of rows.
counterexample: -- impossible: Q1 and Q2 are equivalent for table R(A1 INT, A2 INT, A3 INT)
counterexample_dsp: No counterexample can be produced under the given schema and SQL semantics because there is no database state in which one query returns a row that the other does not.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT X.* FROM R X, R Y
q2: SELECT DISTINCT X.* FROM R X
schema: CREATE TABLE R (X INT);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are actually equivalent.  In Q1 the Cartesian product with the second copy of R only multiplies rows; the final DISTINCT removes those duplicates, leaving exactly the same set of X-values that Q2 returns.  Whenever R is empty both queries return the empty result, and whenever R is non-empty both return the same distinct set of values from R.  Therefore no database instance can make the two queries diverge.
counterexample_dsp: No counterexample is possible under the given schema and constraints, because the two queries are semantically identical for every possible population of R.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT Y.A AS A FROM R X, R Y WHERE X.A = Y.A
q2: SELECT DISTINCT X.A AS A FROM R X
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A INT);
explanation: Q1 performs a self-join on R with the predicate X.A = Y.A. In SQL an equality comparison that involves NULL yields UNKNOWN, which is filtered out by the WHERE clause. Consequently, any row whose A is NULL can never satisfy X.A = Y.A, so NULL values are omitted from Q1’s result. Q2 simply selects DISTINCT A from R and therefore includes NULL (returned once) if it exists. Hence the two queries diverge whenever R contains at least one NULL in column A.
counterexample: INSERT INTO R (A) VALUES (NULL);
counterexample_dsp: Insert a row where A is NULL. Q1 will return no rows (NULL cannot satisfy the equality), while Q2 will return one row containing NULL.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT Y.A1 AS A1, Y.A2 AS A2 FROM R X, R Y WHERE X.A1 = Y.A1 AND X.A2 = Y.A2
q2: SELECT DISTINCT X.A1 AS A1, X.A2 AS A2 FROM R X
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A1 INT, A2 INT);
explanation: Q1 first performs an inner self-join R X  ⋈  R Y on the condition X.A1 = Y.A1 AND X.A2 = Y.A2 and then projects the distinct (Y.A1 , Y.A2) pairs.  Because in SQL any comparison with NULL returns UNKNOWN, a row whose A1 or A2 is NULL never satisfies the equality predicate, so such rows disappear during the join.  Q2, on the other hand, simply returns the distinct pairs that exist in R without any comparison, therefore it keeps rows that contain NULLs.  Hence the two queries differ whenever R contains at least one NULL in A1 or A2.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO R (A1, A2) VALUES (NULL, 1);
INSERT INTO R (A1, A2) VALUES (5, 6);
counterexample_dsp: Insert one tuple that contains a NULL in either column and (optionally) another normal tuple.  The NULL tuple is kept by Q2 but eliminated by the join in Q1, producing different result sets.

q1: SELECT X.A, SUM(X.A + X.B) FROM R X GROUP BY X.A
q2: SELECT Y.A, SUM(Y.A + Y.B) FROM R Y GROUP BY Y.A
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A INT, B INT);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are syntactically identical; they both return, for every distinct value of A in table R, the sum of the expression (A+B) over all rows having that A. The only difference is the choice of table alias (X versus Y), which has no semantic impact. Therefore the queries are equivalent for every possible database instance.
counterexample_dsp: Because the two queries are equivalent, there exists no dataset that can make their results diverge.

q1: SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM R X WHERE X.X > 50) Y WHERE Y.X < 200
q2: SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM R X WHERE X.X < 200) Y WHERE Y.X > 50
schema: CREATE TABLE R (X INT);
explanation: Both queries apply the exact same two predicates (> 50 and < 200) to the same column. The only difference is the order in which the predicates are syntactically written, but because they are independent (no NULL-sensitive functions, no outer joins, no aggregates, no LIMIT, etc.), the logical result is the intersection of the two conditions in both cases (50 < X < 200). Therefore there is no data set that can make the outputs differ.
counterexample_dsp: Not applicable – the queries are logically equivalent for every possible value of R.X (including NULL) under the given schema.

q1: SELECT * FROM R X WHERE X.X > 50 AND X.X < 200
q2: SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM R X WHERE X.X > 50) Y WHERE Y.X < 200
schema: CREATE TABLE R (X INT);
explanation: Q1 applies the two predicates (X > 50) AND (X < 200) in one WHERE-clause.  Q2 applies the same two predicates in two consecutive WHERE-clauses – first (X > 50) in the inner sub-query, then (X < 200) in the outer query.  Because both predicates are ordinary comparisons (no NULL-creating functions, no non-deterministic calls, no outer joins, no DISTINCT, etc.), the logical outcome is exactly the same: a row is returned if and only if X is strictly between 50 and 200.  Therefore the two queries are logically equivalent for every possible instance of table R and no database contents can make them diverge.
counterexample_dsp: No counterexample is possible – the queries are equivalent for all legal rows in R.

q1: SELECT COUNT(*) AS A FROM R X
q2: SELECT COUNT(Y.B) FROM R Y
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A INT, B INT);
explanation: COUNT(*) includes every row in table R, while COUNT(Y.B) only counts rows whose column B is NOT NULL. Therefore, if at least one row has B = NULL, Q1 will count it but Q2 will not, producing different results.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO R (A, B) VALUES (1, NULL);
INSERT INTO R (A, B) VALUES (2, 5);
counterexample_dsp: Insert at least one row where B is NULL (and optionally others where B is non-NULL). The NULL in column B makes COUNT(*) larger than COUNT(B).

q1: SELECT DISTINCT * FROM R X WHERE X.X > 50 OR X.X < 200
schema: CREATE TABLE R (X INT);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are actually equivalent.  For any non-NULL integer X the condition (X > 50 OR X < 200) is always TRUE, therefore Q1 returns every row whose X is not NULL.  Q2 returns the union of rows that satisfy X > 50 and rows that satisfy X < 200, then removes duplicates with an outer DISTINCT; this produces exactly the same set – every non-NULL row.  Rows with X IS NULL are rejected by both queries because each comparison involving NULL is UNKNOWN and the WHERE‐clause requires TRUE.  Since both queries always yield the same result on every possible state of table R, no counter-example database can exist.
counterexample_dsp: Impossible – the queries are logically equivalent under the given schema and three-valued logic; no data can make them differ.

q1: SELECT DEPT.NAME AS DNAME, COUNT(*) AS C FROM DEPT AS DEPT GROUP BY DEPT.NAME HAVING DEPT.NAME = 10
q2: SELECT T2.DNAME, T2.CNT AS C FROM (SELECT DEPT0.NAME AS DNAME, COUNT(*) AS CNT FROM DEPT AS DEPT0 GROUP BY DEPT0.NAME) AS T2 WHERE T2.DNAME = 10
schema: CREATE TABLE DEPT (DEPTNO INT, NAME INT);
explanation: Q1 filters the grouped result with HAVING NAME = 10, while Q2 first creates exactly the same grouped result in a sub-query and then filters it with WHERE DNAME = 10. Because NAME is the only grouping column and the literal 10 is compared in exactly the same way in both places, every group that survives (or is rejected) in Q1 will also survive (or be rejected) in Q2. There is no SQL-standard situation (including NULL handling) in which the two queries return different rows or counts, so they are logically equivalent.
counterexample_dsp: No data set can make the two queries diverge, therefore a counterexample does not exist.

q1: SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM R X WHERE X.X > 0) Y WHERE Y.X > 0
q2: SELECT * FROM R X WHERE X.X > 0
schema: CREATE TABLE R (X INT);
explanation: Q1 first applies the predicate X > 0 inside a derived-table, then applies the exact same predicate again in the outer query. Q2 applies that predicate once directly. Because the predicate (X > 0) is deterministic and refers only to the values of column X, re-applying it cannot add or remove rows – it is simply redundant. Hence, for every possible content of table R, the two queries always return exactly the same set of rows. Therefore no database state can make their results differ.
counterexample_dsp: Impossible – there is no condition (NULL handling, duplicates, outer join, grouping, etc.) that can make the double application of the same deterministic filter diverge from a single application. The queries are equivalent for all instances of table R.

q1: SELECT * FROM A X WHERE X.C IN (SELECT Y.C FROM A Y)
q2: SELECT * FROM A X
schema: CREATE TABLE A (C INT);
explanation: Q1 keeps a row only when X.C matches **(=)** at least one non-NULL value returned by the sub-query.  If X.C is NULL the comparison "NULL = Y.C" is UNKNOWN, therefore the IN predicate is not satisfied and that row is filtered out.  Q2 applies no such predicate and therefore returns every row, including those whose C is NULL.  Hence the two queries differ whenever table A contains a row with C = NULL.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO A (C) VALUES (NULL);
INSERT INTO A (C) VALUES (1);
counterexample_dsp: Have at least one row in A where C is NULL (and optionally another non-NULL row).  The NULL row is returned by Q2 but suppressed by Q1, because "NULL IN (subquery)" evaluates to UNKNOWN/false.

q1: SELECT X.A1 AS A1, X.A2 AS A2, Y.B1 AS B1, Y.B2 AS B2 FROM A X, B Y WHERE X.A1 = Y.B1
q2: SELECT Y.A1 AS A1, Y.A2 AS A2, X.B1 AS B1, X.B2 AS B2 FROM B X, A Y WHERE Y.A1 = X.B1
schema:
CREATE TABLE A (A1 INT, A2 INT);
CREATE TABLE B (B1 INT, B2 INT);
explanation: No counter-example can be produced, because Q1 and Q2 are logically identical. Both queries perform an inner join between table A and table B on the equality A.A1 = B.B1 and return exactly the same four columns (A1, A2 coming from A and B1, B2 coming from B).  The difference in the FROM-clause order and the aliases has no impact on the join condition, duplicate handling, or NULL semantics.  Therefore the result multiset is guaranteed to be the same for every possible database instance.
counterexample_dsp: Impossible – the queries are equivalent under all circumstances allowed by the schema, so there is no data that can make them diverge.

q1: SELECT * FROM R1 X, (SELECT * FROM R2 UNION ALL SELECT * FROM R3) Y
explanation: Q1 builds a Cartesian product between R1 and the UNION ALL of R2 and R3.  Q2 performs the same two Cartesian products separately and then appends them with UNION ALL.  For every tuple multiplicity in the three tables the resulting multiset counts and values are |R1|·(|R2|+|R3|) in both queries, so the two result-bags are always identical.  Because the queries are algebraically identical, no database state can make them diverge.
counterexample_dsp: Not possible – the queries are equivalent for every legal instance of the given schema, so there is no data that can make their results differ.

q1: SELECT X.B AS XB, Y.B AS YB FROM R1 X, R2 Y
q2: SELECT X1.XB AS XB, Y1.YB AS YB FROM (SELECT X.B AS XB FROM R1 X) X1, (SELECT Y.B AS YB FROM R2 Y) Y1
schema:
CREATE TABLE R1 (A INT, B INT);
CREATE TABLE R2 (A INT, B INT);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 both take every row of R1 and every row of R2 and build the Cartesian product of the two tables, returning the pair (R1.B , R2.B) for every such combination.  The sub-queries in Q2 neither filter, group, nor deduplicate – they merely project the same column B, keeping every duplicate and NULL exactly as it appears in the base tables.  Therefore, for every possible state of the database the two queries produce the same multiset of result rows; no construct in either query can introduce a divergence.
counterexample_dsp: Impossible – the queries are equivalent for every legal population of R1 and R2, so no dataset can make them differ.

q1: SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM R UNION ALL SELECT * FROM S) X
schema:
CREATE TABLE R (X INT);
CREATE TABLE S (X INT);
explanation: The two queries are definition-ally the same: both return every row of R followed by every row of S (UNION ALL keeps duplicates and keeps the order of its left/right operands unless an ORDER BY is added later). Parenthesising the UNION ALL inside a derived table (Q1) does not change either the row set or the column names, because the derived table’s column list inherits the original column names (R.X / S.X). Therefore there is no condition – NULLs, duplicates, missing rows, etc. – under which Q1 and Q2 can diverge. A counterexample cannot be constructed for the supplied schema.
counterexample: -- No INSERTs possible, the queries are always equivalent.
counterexample_dsp: Not applicable – the queries are equivalent for every possible population of tables R and S.

q1: SELECT * FROM A X, (SELECT * FROM B Y WHERE Y.X < 100) Z WHERE X.X = Z.X
q2: SELECT * FROM A X, B Y WHERE X.X = Y.X AND Y.X < 100
schema:
CREATE TABLE A (X INT);
CREATE TABLE B (X INT);
explanation: The two queries are logically identical: both (1) filter table B so that only rows with X < 100 survive, and (2) inner-join those surviving B-rows with table A on equality of the X column.  They employ the same predicates and the same (inner) join condition; the sub-query in Q1 is uncorrelated and merely materialises the very same set of B-rows that Q2 filters in the WHERE clause.  Because there is no construct whose semantics can diverge between the two formulations (no NULL-sensitive outer joins, DISTINCT, aggregation, ORDER/LIMIT, etc.), they always return the same multiset of result rows.
counterexample_dsp: No counter-example can be produced: for every possible population of tables A and B that satisfies the schema (the only constraint is that X may be NULL), the result bags of Q1 and Q2 are guaranteed to coincide.

q1: SELECT X.A AS A FROM X X, Y Y WHERE X.K = Y.K
q2: SELECT X1.A AS X1A FROM (SELECT X.A AS A, X.K AS K FROM X X) X1, Y Y WHERE X1.K = Y.K
schema:
CREATE TABLE X (A INT, K INT);
CREATE TABLE Y (A INT, K INT);
explanation:
The sub-query in Q2 is only a straight projection of X (no DISTINCT, filtering, aggregation, etc.). Therefore Q2 joins the very same rows of X with Y on the same equality predicate (X.K = Y.K) and returns the very same values of X.A (only the output column name differs). Because every step that could possibly change the result (filters, duplicate elimination, NULL handling, outer vs. inner joins, etc.) is identical in the two queries, they always yield the same multiset of data values.

Hence Q1 and Q2 are logically equivalent for every possible database state; a counter-example does not exist.
counterexample_dsp: Not applicable – the queries are equivalent under all circumstances permitted by the schema.

q1: SELECT * FROM R1 X, (SELECT * FROM R2 Y WHERE Y.X > 0) Z
q2: SELECT * FROM R1 X, R2 Y WHERE Y.X > 0
schema:
CREATE TABLE R1 (X INT);
CREATE TABLE R2 (X INT);
explanation: Q1 first filters R2 on the condition X > 0 and then cross-joins that reduced R2 with every row of R1.  Q2 first cross-joins every row of R1 with every row of R2 and then applies the very same filter (X > 0) that only references R2.  Because the predicate involves no columns of R1, pushing the predicate before or after the cross product is algebraically identical (σ(R1×R2)  ≡  R1×σ(R2) when the predicate contains only R2 attributes).  Consequently, for every possible database instance the two queries always return exactly the same multiset of rows.  Therefore no counterexample data can exist.
counterexample: -- impossible: Q1 and Q2 are equivalent, so no INSERTs can make them diverge
counterexample_dsp: Not applicable – the queries are logically equivalent for all inputs, so no data can make their results differ.

q1: SELECT X.A + X.B, X.A/X.B AS A FROM R X
q2: SELECT Y.A + Y.B, Y.A/Y.B AS A FROM R Y
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A INT, B INT);
explanation: The two queries perform the exact same projection (A + B and A / B) over the same single table R. The only difference is the choice of correlation name (X versus Y), which has no impact on the result set. Since they use identical expressions, have no joins, grouping, filters, or NULL-sensitive predicates that differ, there is no circumstance under the given schema in which Q1 and Q2 can return different results.
counterexample: -- impossible to produce: queries are equivalent, so no INSERTs can make them diverge
counterexample_dsp: No counter-example is possible: irrespective of the data in R, both queries always yield identical rows and column values because they are syntactically and semantically equivalent.

q1: SELECT * FROM A X UNION ALL SELECT * FROM A X WHERE FALSE
q2: SELECT * FROM A X
schema: CREATE TABLE A (X INT);
explanation: Q1 first returns every row of table A. The UNION ALL then concatenates the result of a second SELECT that is filtered by WHERE FALSE, which always yields zero rows. Therefore the UNION ALL adds nothing. Q1 always produces exactly the same multiset of rows as the plain SELECT in Q2. Because the second branch of Q1 can never contribute any row under any database state, Q1 and Q2 are semantically equivalent and can never diverge.
counterexample_dsp: Not applicable – no conceivable population of table A can cause the queries to differ, since the second sub-query in Q1 is hard-coded to return 0 rows (WHERE FALSE).

q1: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(C.CREDITS) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(C.CREDITS) > 10 AND COUNT(DISTINCT C.CREDITS) > 5
q2: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(C.CREDITS) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(C.CREDITS) > 10 AND COUNT(DISTINCT C.CREDITS) > 8
explanation: Both queries aggregate COURSE rows per department after an inner-join with DEPARTMENT.  They keep only those departments whose total credits exceed 10.  The only difference is the second HAVING predicate: Q1 keeps a group when it has more than 5 distinct credit values, while Q2 requires more than 8.  Therefore any department whose group contains 6–8 distinct credit values will appear in Q1 but be filtered out by Q2.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO DEPARTMENT (DEPT_NAME, BUILDING, BUDGET) VALUES (1, 10, 10000);

INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES
  (101, 101, 1, 1),  -- credit value 1
  (102, 102, 1, 2),  -- credit value 2
  (103, 103, 1, 3),  -- credit value 3
  (104, 104, 1, 4),  -- credit value 4
  (105, 105, 1, 5),  -- credit value 5
  (106, 106, 1, 6);  -- credit value 6
counterexample_dsp: Create one department (dept 1) and six courses that all belong to that department.  Give the six courses mutually different CREDIT values 1–6.  This yields SUM(CREDITS)=21 (>10) and COUNT(DISTINCT CREDITS)=6 ( >5 but not >8).  Hence the group passes Q1 and fails Q2.

q1: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, AVG(I.SALARY) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (C.COURSE_ID = T.COURSE_ID) INNER JOIN INSTRUCTOR I ON (D.DEPT_NAME = I.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING AVG(I.SALARY)>50000 AND COUNT(DISTINCT I.SALARY)=4
q2: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, AVG(I.SALARY) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (C.COURSE_ID = T.COURSE_ID) INNER JOIN INSTRUCTOR I ON (D.DEPT_NAME = I.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING AVG(I.SALARY)>50000 AND COUNT(DISTINCT I.SALARY)>4
explanation:
The two queries are identical except for the HAVING-clause predicate on the number of distinct instructor salaries found per department.
 • Q1 keeps a department when AVG(I.SALARY) > 50000 AND COUNT(DISTINCT I.SALARY) = 4.
 • Q2 keeps a department when AVG(I.SALARY) > 50000 AND COUNT(DISTINCT I.SALARY) > 4.
Therefore any department that has exactly four different salaries (and an average salary above 50 000) will be returned by Q1 but filtered out by Q2, while departments with more than four different salaries will be returned by Q2 but not by Q1.
counterexample_dsp: Create one department that has exactly four instructors with four different salaries (all above 50 000).  Add one course in that department and one teaches-row for that course so the joins succeed.  The GROUP BY produces a single group with COUNT(DISTINCT salary) = 4 and AVG(salary) > 50 000, making Q1 return the row and Q2 return none.

q1: SELECT STUDENT.ID FROM COURSE NATURAL JOIN DEPARTMENT NATURAL JOIN STUDENT NATURAL JOIN TAKES NATURAL JOIN SECTION GROUP BY STUDENT.ID,STUDENT.DEPT_NAME HAVING COUNT(DEPT_NAME) >= 2
q2: SELECT STUDENT.ID FROM COURSE NATURAL JOIN DEPARTMENT NATURAL JOIN STUDENT NATURAL JOIN TAKES NATURAL JOIN SECTION GROUP BY STUDENT.ID HAVING COUNT(DEPT_NAME) >= 2
explanation:
Both queries start with the same 5-way natural inner join.  After the join they aggregate.
• Q1 groups by (STUDENT.ID , STUDENT.DEPT_NAME).  A student that appears under two different department names is split into two different groups.
• Q2 groups only by STUDENT.ID, so every row with the same ID – no matter which department row it came from – is put into one single group.
The HAVING clause keeps groups that contain at least two joined rows.  Therefore, when the *same* student-id can be associated with rows coming from *different* departments, Q2 will count the union of those rows (≥2) and return the id, while Q1 will see two separate groups that each have a count <2 and will not return anything.  Hence the two queries are not equivalent.
counterexample_dsp: Create two STUDENT rows that share the same ID but have different DEPT_NAME values (no PK is declared, so this is legal).  Add matching DEPARTMENT and COURSE rows for each department, one SECTION per course, and make the student take each section.  The join therefore produces exactly one joined row for each (ID, DEPT_NAME) pair.  Q1 ends up with two groups of size 1 (filtered out), whereas Q2 has one group of size 2 (kept).

q1: SELECT DISTINCT DEPT_NAME FROM COURSE WHERE CREDITS = (SELECT MAX(CREDITS) FROM COURSE NATURAL JOIN DEPARTMENT WHERE TITLE='CS' GROUP BY DEPT_NAME HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT COURSE_ID)>4)
q2: SELECT DEPT_NAME FROM COURSE WHERE CREDITS = (SELECT MAX(CREDITS) FROM COURSE NATURAL JOIN DEPARTMENT WHERE TITLE='CS' GROUP BY DEPT_NAME HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT COURSE_ID)>4)
explanation: The only difference between the two queries is the DISTINCT keyword that appears in Q1 but not in Q2.  • Both queries first compute, for every department that offers more than 4 courses whose TITLE is 'CS', the maximum number of credits in that department.  • Suppose this sub-query returns a single value M (because exactly one department satisfies the GROUP BY / HAVING condition).  • The outer query then looks in COURSE for every row whose CREDITS = M and returns that row’s DEPT_NAME.  Because Q1 adds DISTINCT, it eliminates duplicate department names coming from several courses that all have CREDITS = M, whereas Q2 keeps every duplicate.  Therefore, whenever at least two different COURSE rows of the same department have the maximal credit value M, Q2 will output that department name more than once while Q1 will output it only once.
counterexample_dsp: Have one department (say 1) with 5 courses titled 'CS'.  Two of those courses must share the maximal credit value (e.g., both have 5 credits).  The sub-query therefore returns a single value 5.  The outer query sees two rows whose CREDITS=5 and DEPT_NAME=1, so Q2 returns the department twice, while Q1 returns it once because of DISTINCT.

q1: SELECT STUDENT.ID, STUDENT.NAME FROM STUDENT JOIN (SELECT TAKES.ID, S.TIME_SLOT_ID, S.YEAR FROM TAKES JOIN SECTION AS S ON TAKES.COURSE_ID = S.COURSE_ID AND TAKES.SEC_ID = S.SEC_ID GROUP BY TAKES.ID, S.TIME_SLOT_ID, S.YEAR HAVING COUNT(S.TIME_SLOT_ID) > 1) AS A ON STUDENT.ID = A.ID GROUP BY STUDENT.ID, STUDENT.NAME HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT STUDENT.ID) > 2
q2: SELECT STUDENT.ID, STUDENT.NAME FROM STUDENT JOIN (SELECT TAKES.ID, S.TIME_SLOT_ID, S.YEAR FROM TAKES JOIN SECTION AS S ON TAKES.COURSE_ID = S.COURSE_ID AND TAKES.SEC_ID = S.SEC_ID GROUP BY TAKES.ID, S.TIME_SLOT_ID, S.YEAR HAVING SUM(S.TIME_SLOT_ID) > 1) AS A ON STUDENT.ID = A.ID GROUP BY STUDENT.ID, STUDENT.NAME HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT STUDENT.ID) > 2
explanation: The two queries are actually *logically equivalent* (they always return the empty result set).  After the join, each result row still carries the single STUDENT.ID value coming from the STUDENT table.  Because the outer query groups by STUDENT.ID and STUDENT.NAME, every group contains only one (distinct) STUDENT.ID value.  Therefore COUNT(DISTINCT STUDENT.ID) is at most 1 for every group, and the HAVING clause “COUNT(DISTINCT STUDENT.ID) > 2” can never be satisfied.  This makes both Q1 and Q2 return no rows, regardless of any differences in the inner sub-query (COUNT vs. SUM on TIME_SLOT_ID).  Consequently no database instance can make the results diverge.
counterexample: -- no INSERTs are needed because no possible data can distinguish the two queries
counterexample_dsp: Not applicable – the HAVING condition guarantees that both queries are empty for every possible database.  Hence there exists no counterexample.

q1: SELECT SUM(T) AS SU FROM (SELECT YEAR AS T FROM TEACHES NATURAL JOIN INSTRUCTOR GROUP BY YEAR, COURSE_ID HAVING COUNT(ID)>4) AS TEMP GROUP BY T
q2: SELECT SUM(T) AS SU FROM (SELECT YEAR AS T FROM TEACHES NATURAL JOIN INSTRUCTOR GROUP BY YEAR HAVING COUNT(ID)>4) AS TEMP GROUP BY T
explanation: Inside the sub-query Q1 groups by (YEAR, COURSE_ID) whereas Q2 groups only by YEAR. If, in the same year, two (or more) different courses each have more than four teaching-rows, Q1 will return that YEAR once for every qualifying course, while Q2 will return it only once. Because the outer query sums T again after grouping by T, Q1 will multiply the year value by the number of qualifying courses; Q2 will not. Hence the two queries are not equivalent.
counterexample_dsp: Create one year (2022) with two different courses (101 and 102). Each course is taught by five different instructors (so every (YEAR,COURSE_ID) group has COUNT(ID)=5>4). The total number of rows for the year is 10, therefore Q1 will output 4044 (=2022*2) while Q2 will output 2022.

q1: WITH S AS (SELECT ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR FROM TAKES NATURAL JOIN SECTION GROUP BY ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR HAVING COUNT(TIME_SLOT_ID)>4) SELECT DISTINCT ID,NAME FROM S NATURAL JOIN STUDENT
q2: WITH S AS (SELECT ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR FROM TAKES NATURAL JOIN SECTION GROUP BY ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR HAVING COUNT(TIME_SLOT_ID)>5) SELECT DISTINCT ID,NAME FROM S NATURAL JOIN STUDENT
explanation:
Both queries look for students who have taken “many” sections that happen to be scheduled in the same time-slot and year.  The only difference is the threshold in the HAVING clause:
 • Q1 keeps groups with COUNT(*) > 4 (≥5 rows)
 • Q2 keeps groups with COUNT(*) > 5 (≥6 rows)
Therefore every result of Q2 is also a result of Q1, but a group that occurs exactly 5 times appears only in Q1.  Creating such a 5-row group is enough to show the two queries are not equivalent.
counterexample_dsp: Make one student who takes exactly 5 different sections that all share the same TIME_SLOT_ID and YEAR.  The join TAKES ⋈ SECTION will produce 5 matching rows for that (ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR) combination, so Q1 (COUNT>4) will return the student while Q2 (COUNT>5) will not.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT DEPT_NAME FROM COURSE JOIN (SELECT MAX(CREDITS) AS MAX_CREDITS FROM COURSE) AS A ON COURSE.CREDITS = A.MAX_CREDITS
q2: SELECT DISTINCT DEPT_NAME FROM COURSE JOIN (SELECT MAX(CREDITS) AS MAX_CREDITS FROM COURSE GROUP BY DEPT_NAME) AS A ON COURSE.CREDITS = A.MAX_CREDITS
explanation:
Q1 looks for the (global) highest number of credits that exists in the COURSE table and returns the departments that offer courses with exactly that **single** maximum value.
Q2 first computes the highest-credit value **per department**, then joins that *set* of values back to COURSE.  Any course whose credit load equals **any** department’s local maximum is kept, even if that value is *not* the maximum for its own department.  Therefore departments whose own maximum is below the global maximum can still appear in Q2 if their local-max value coincides with another department’s maximum.  This cannot happen in Q1, so the result sets can differ.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES
  (1, 101, 10, 4),  -- Dept 10, local max 4
  (2, 102, 10, 3),  -- Dept 10, lower credit
  (3, 201, 20, 5);  -- Dept 20, global max 5
counterexample_dsp: Two departments.  Dept A offers courses with 3 and 4 credits (so its local max = 4).  Dept B offers one course with 5 credits (global max = 5).  Q1 returns only Dept B (because 5 is the global max).  Q2 collects the set {4,5} of per-dept maxima, joins on credits IN (4,5), and therefore returns Dept A and Dept B – a different result set.

q1: SELECT C.NAME FROM CARRIERS AS C JOIN FLIGHTS AS F ON C.CID = F.CARRIER_ID GROUP BY C.NAME, F.YEAR, F.MONTH_ID, F.DAY_OF_MONTH HAVING COUNT(F.FID) > 1000
q2: SELECT C.NAME FROM CARRIERS AS C JOIN FLIGHTS AS F ON C.CID = F.CARRIER_ID GROUP BY C.NAME, F.DAY_OF_MONTH HAVING COUNT(C.CID) > 1000
explanation: Q1 counts flights per carrier *per (year, month, day-of-month)*, while Q2 counts flights per carrier *per (day-of-month)*, ignoring year and month. Therefore totals can accumulate across several months/years in Q2 but not in Q1. If every (year,month,day) subgroup has ≤1000 rows, Q1 returns nothing, yet the sum of those subgroups can exceed 1000 so that Q2 still returns the carrier.
counterexample_dsp: Make two flight records for the same carrier on the same day-of-month (15) but different months.  Add 900 duplicate carrier rows (same CID/NAME) so that the join produces 900 copies of each flight.  Each (year,month,day) subgroup then contains 900 rows (<1001) so Q1 finds none.  Across the two months Q2 sees 1800 rows (>1000) for day 15 and therefore outputs the carrier name.

q1: SELECT C.NAME FROM CARRIERS AS C JOIN FLIGHTS AS F ON C.CID = F.CARRIER_ID GROUP BY C.CID, C.NAME, F.YEAR, F.MONTH_ID, F.DAY_OF_MONTH HAVING COUNT(F.FID) > 1000
q2: SELECT C.NAME FROM CARRIERS AS C JOIN FLIGHTS AS F ON C.CID = F.CARRIER_ID GROUP BY C.NAME, F.DAY_OF_MONTH HAVING COUNT(F.FID) > 1000
explanation:
Both queries join CARRIERS and FLIGHTS and then count the number of joined rows, returning the carrier name(s) whose count is larger than 1000.  
• Q1 groups by C.CID, C.NAME, F.YEAR, F.MONTH_ID, F.DAY_OF_MONTH – every (carrier-id, exact calendar day) is counted separately.
• Q2 groups only by C.NAME and F.DAY_OF_MONTH – it ignores the carrier id and it also ignores the month and year.
If the same carrier flies many times on the 1-st day of several different months (or if several different CIDs share the same NAME), Q2 will add all those rows together, while Q1 will keep them in separate groups.  Consequently Q2 can pass the “> 1000” threshold when Q1 does not.  The test data below exploits this difference: 600 flights on 1-Jan-2023 and 500 flights on 1-Feb-2023 for the same carrier.  Q2 sees 1100 flights (600+500) and returns the carrier name; Q1 sees only 600 or 500 per group and returns nothing.
counterexample_dsp: One carrier (CID = 1, NAME = 1).  600 flights on 2023-01-01 and 500 flights on 2023-02-01 (same DAY_OF_MONTH = 1).  Each (year, month, day) group has ≤1000 flights, so Q1 returns no row.  Q2 aggregates the two months together (because it does not group by year or month) and sees 1100 flights, therefore it outputs NAME = 1.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT F.ORIGIN_CITY, F.DEST_CITY, F.ACTUAL_TIME FROM FLIGHTS AS F JOIN (SELECT A.ORIGIN_CITY, MAX(A.ACTUAL_TIME) AS MAX_TIME FROM FLIGHTS AS A GROUP BY A.ORIGIN_CITY) AS X ON F.ORIGIN_CITY = X.ORIGIN_CITY AND F.ACTUAL_TIME = X.MAX_TIME
q2: SELECT S.ORIGIN_CITY, F2.DEST_CITY, MAX(F2.ACTUAL_TIME) FROM (SELECT F1.ORIGIN_CITY, MAX(F1.ACTUAL_TIME) AS MAX_TIME FROM FLIGHTS AS F1 GROUP BY F1.ORIGIN_CITY) AS S JOIN FLIGHTS AS F2 ON S.ORIGIN_CITY = F2.ORIGIN_CITY AND F2.ACTUAL_TIME = S.MAX_TIME GROUP BY S.ORIGIN_CITY, F2.DEST_CITY
explanation:
Both queries first determine, for every ORIGIN_CITY, the maximum ACTUAL_TIME that occurs in table FLIGHTS.  Each query then returns (ORIGIN_CITY , DEST_CITY , that-maximum-time) for every flight whose ACTUAL_TIME equals this maximum.  
•  In Q1 this is done by joining FLIGHTS with the MAX-per-origin sub-query and then using DISTINCT to eliminate duplicate rows that might arise from identical flights.
•  In Q2 the same join is performed first; afterwards the result is GROUPed BY ORIGIN_CITY and DEST_CITY and MAX(F2.ACTUAL_TIME) is projected.  Because the join predicate already guarantees F2.ACTUAL_TIME = S.MAX_TIME, the aggregate again yields exactly the same value that appears in Q1.  The GROUP BY therefore collapses the very same duplicates that DISTINCT removes in Q1.
Consequently, for every possible database state the two result sets are identical – there is no condition (NULL handling, duplicate rows, ties in the maximum, etc.) that makes one query return a row the other one does not.  Hence the queries are equivalent and no counter-example can be constructed.
counterexample_dsp: A counterexample is impossible because the two queries are equivalent for all possible contents of table FLIGHTS (and none of the other tables are referenced at all).

q1: SELECT DISTINCT F.ORIGIN_CITY, F.DEST_CITY, F.ACTUAL_TIME FROM FLIGHTS AS F JOIN (SELECT A.ORIGIN_CITY, MAX(A.ACTUAL_TIME) AS MAX_TIME FROM FLIGHTS AS A GROUP BY A.ORIGIN_CITY) AS X ON F.ORIGIN_CITY = X.ORIGIN_CITY AND F.ACTUAL_TIME = X.MAX_TIME
q2: SELECT P.ORIGIN_CITY, P.DEST_CITY, P.ACTUAL_TIME FROM (SELECT F1.ORIGIN_CITY, F1.DEST_CITY, F1.ACTUAL_TIME, MAX(F2.ACTUAL_TIME) AS MAX_ACTUAL_TIME FROM FLIGHTS AS F1 JOIN FLIGHTS AS F2 ON F1.ORIGIN_CITY = F2.ORIGIN_CITY GROUP BY F1.ORIGIN_CITY, F1.DEST_CITY, F1.ACTUAL_TIME) AS P WHERE P.ACTUAL_TIME = P.MAX_ACTUAL_TIME
explanation:
Although both statements seem to return “the flights whose ACTUAL_TIME is the largest for their ORIGIN_CITY”, they do it in slightly-different ways.  Q1 first finds the maximal time per origin (subquery X) and then keeps every flight that *has exactly that time*.  Consequently, two flights that share the same ORIGIN_CITY and the same ACTUAL_TIME automatically survive – even if they are completely identical rows.

Q2, however, re-computes the maximum inside a GROUP BY that already collapses duplicates of (ORIGIN_CITY, DEST_CITY, ACTUAL_TIME).  Therefore, if the table FLIGHTS contains two (or more) **completely identical rows** that are maximal for their origin, Q1 will output one copy (because of DISTINCT) while Q2 will output none – the identical rows merge into one group whose ACTUAL_TIME no longer equals MAX_ACTUAL_TIME (the aggregated value now comes from the duplicated partner rows).

Hence, when the table contains at least two identical maximal rows, the two queries differ.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO FLIGHTS (FID, ORIGIN_CITY, DEST_CITY, ACTUAL_TIME) VALUES
  (1, 10, 20, 300),   -- first copy of the maximal flight
  (2, 10, 20, 300),   -- second identical copy (causes the divergence)
  (3, 10, 30, 250);   -- smaller flight so max is really 300
counterexample_dsp: Create one origin city with two *identical* maximal flight rows and another smaller-time row.  The duplicated maximal rows survive the JOIN in Q1 but collapse inside the GROUP BY of Q2, so the equality “ACTUAL_TIME = MAX_ACTUAL_TIME” becomes false and Q2 returns nothing, whereas Q1 still returns the (deduplicated) maximal flight.

q1: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(C.CREDITS) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(C.CREDITS)>10 AND COUNT(C.CREDITS)>5
q2: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(C.CREDITS) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(C.CREDITS)>10 AND COUNT(C.CREDITS)>8
explanation: Both queries aggregate COURSE rows per department and keep only those groups whose total credits are greater than 10.  They differ only in the COUNT() condition: Q1 keeps departments that offer more than 5 courses, whereas Q2 requires more than 8 courses.  Therefore, a department that has 6-8 courses (inclusive) and whose summed credits are still >10 will appear in Q1 but be filtered out by Q2.
counterexample_dsp: Create one department (dept_name = 1).  Insert 7 courses for that department, each worth 2 credits.  The group produced for dept 1 has SUM(credits)=14 (>10) and COUNT(credits)=7 ( >5 but not >8 ).  Hence Q1 returns the row, Q2 does not.

q1: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(I.SALARY) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN INSTRUCTOR I ON (D.DEPT_NAME = I.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(I.SALARY)>100 AND MAX(I.SALARY)<75
q2: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(I.SALARY) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN INSTRUCTOR I ON (D.DEPT_NAME = I.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(I.SALARY)>=100 AND MAX(I.SALARY)<75
explanation: Both queries aggregate salaries of instructors per department, but Q1 keeps a group only when the total salary is strictly greater than 100, while Q2 keeps it when the total is greater than or equal to 100. Therefore they differ precisely when SUM(I.SALARY) is exactly 100 (and MAX(I.SALARY) is still below 75).
counterexample_dsp: Create one department that owns one course and exactly two instructors, each paid 50. The join yields two rows for that department; SUM(salary)=100 and MAX(salary)=50 (<75). Q1 excludes the department (100 is not >100) whereas Q2 includes it (100 ≥100).

q1: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(D.BUDGET) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (C.COURSE_ID = T.COURSE_ID) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(D.BUDGET)>100000 AND COUNT(D.BUDGET)>10
q2: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(D.BUDGET) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (C.COURSE_ID = T.COURSE_ID) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(D.BUDGET)>100000 AND COUNT(DISTINCT D.BUDGET)>10
explanation: Both queries group the joined COURSE-DEPARTMENT-TEACHES rows by C.DEPT_NAME and keep only those departments whose total budget exceeds 100 000.  The difference is that Q1 uses COUNT(D.BUDGET) (every joined row is counted) while Q2 uses COUNT(DISTINCT D.BUDGET) (duplicates of the same budget value are collapsed before counting).  When many joined rows repeat the same budget value, the ordinary COUNT can be > 10 while the DISTINCT-COUNT stays ≤ 10, so Q1 keeps the department and Q2 discards it.
counterexample_dsp: Create one department with a budget of 10 000, one course that belongs to it and eleven TEACHES rows for that course.  The join therefore produces 11 rows that all carry the same budget value (10 000).  SUM(BUDGET)=110 000 and COUNT(BUDGET)=11, so Q1’s HAVING clause is satisfied.  COUNT(DISTINCT BUDGET)=1, so Q2’s HAVING clause fails.  No other data are needed.

q1: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, AVG(I.SALARY) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (C.COURSE_ID = T.COURSE_ID) INNER JOIN INSTRUCTOR I ON (D.DEPT_NAME = I.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING AVG(I.SALARY)>50000 AND COUNT(DISTINCT I.SALARY)=4
q2: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, AVG(I.SALARY) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (C.COURSE_ID = T.COURSE_ID) INNER JOIN INSTRUCTOR I ON (D.DEPT_NAME = I.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING AVG(I.SALARY)>50000 AND COUNT(DISTINCT I.SALARY)>4
explanation: Both queries aggregate instructors’ salaries per department that actually has at least one course and at least one TEACHES row (because of the joins).  The only difference is the HAVING clause:  Q1 keeps a department when it has exactly 4 distinct salary values (COUNT(DISTINCT I.SALARY)=4); Q2 keeps a department when it has more than 4 distinct salary values (COUNT(DISTINCT I.SALARY)>4).  Therefore any department that has precisely 4 different salaries (and average salary > 50 000) will appear in Q1 but be filtered out by Q2, so the two queries are not equivalent.
counterexample_dsp: Create one department that owns one course which is taught at least once (so the joins succeed).  Put exactly four instructors in that department with distinct salaries all above 50 000.  The group for that department will have   AVG(I.SALARY)=75 000 > 50 000 and COUNT(DISTINCT I.SALARY)=4, so Q1 returns it whereas Q2 does not.

q1: SELECT T.SEMESTER, SUM(C.CREDITS) FROM DEPARTMENT D INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (D.BUDGET = T.YEAR + 4) INNER JOIN COURSE C ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY T.SEMESTER HAVING AVG(C.CREDITS)>2 AND COUNT(D.BUILDING)=2
q2: SELECT T.SEMESTER, SUM(C.CREDITS) FROM DEPARTMENT D INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (D.BUDGET = T.YEAR + 4) INNER JOIN COURSE C ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY T.SEMESTER HAVING AVG(C.CREDITS)>2 AND COUNT(D.BUILDING)>=2
explanation:
Both queries join DEPARTMENT-TEACHES-COURSE, then group the result by T.SEMESTER and keep only the groups whose average course credits is > 2.  The only difference is the COUNT test in the HAVING clause:
  • Q1 keeps groups where COUNT(D.BUILDING) = 2
  • Q2 keeps groups where COUNT(D.BUILDING) ≥ 2
Therefore a semester that appears 3 (or more) times in the joined rows (so count = 3) will be returned by Q2 but filtered-out by Q1.
counterexample_dsp:
Create one department D, one course C that belongs to D (credits=4), and three TEACHES rows for the same semester that all join with D and C.  The join produces three rows for that semester.  For the group:
  COUNT(D.BUILDING) = 3  → satisfies ">= 2" but not "= 2"
  AVG(C.CREDITS)   = 4   → satisfies > 2
Thus Q2 returns the semester while Q1 returns nothing.

q1: SELECT ID FROM COURSE NATURAL JOIN DEPARTMENT NATURAL JOIN STUDENT NATURAL JOIN TAKES NATURAL JOIN SECTION GROUP BY ID,DEPT_NAME HAVING COUNT(DEPT_NAME) >= 2
q2: SELECT ID FROM COURSE NATURAL JOIN DEPARTMENT NATURAL JOIN STUDENT NATURAL JOIN TAKES NATURAL JOIN SECTION GROUP BY ID HAVING COUNT(DEPT_NAME) >= 2
explanation: Q1 forms groups on (ID , DEPT_NAME).  A student is returned only when at least two joined rows belong to the SAME department.  Q2 groups only on ID, so any two (or more) joined rows – even if they come from different departments – already satisfy the HAVING clause.  Therefore a student who has exactly one joined row per department (two different departments) appears in Q2 but not in Q1.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO DEPARTMENT (DEPT_NAME, BUILDING, BUDGET) VALUES
  (10, 1, 100000),
  (20, 2, 100000);

INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES
  (1, 101, 10, 3),
  (2, 102, 20, 3);

-- same student ID appears in two different departments
INSERT INTO STUDENT (ID, NAME, DEPT_NAME, TOT_CRED) VALUES
  (100, 1001, 10, 30),
  (100, 1001, 20, 30);

INSERT INTO SECTION (COURSE_ID, SEC_ID, YEAR, BUILDING, ROOM_NUMBER, TIME_SLOT_ID) VALUES
  (1, 1, 2023, 1, 101, 1),
  (2, 1, 2023, 1, 102, 1);

INSERT INTO TAKES (ID, COURSE_ID, SEC_ID, YEAR, GRADE) VALUES
  (100, 1, 1, 2023, 4),  -- course from dept 10
  (100, 2, 1, 2023, 3);  -- course from dept 20
counterexample_dsp: Create one student that is recorded twice in STUDENT (same ID, different DEPT_NAME).  Give that student one TAKE for a course offered by each of the two departments.  The natural joins therefore yield two result-rows: (ID=100, DEPT_NAME=10) and (ID=100, DEPT_NAME=20).  Q2 sees two rows for ID 100 (COUNT=2) and returns the ID; Q1 splits them into two separate (ID,DEPT_NAME) groups of size 1 and returns nothing.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT DEPT_NAME FROM COURSE WHERE CREDITS = (SELECT MAX(CREDITS) FROM COURSE NATURAL JOIN DEPARTMENT WHERE TITLE='CS' GROUP BY DEPT_NAME HAVING COUNT(COURSE_ID)>2)
q2: SELECT DEPT_NAME FROM COURSE WHERE CREDITS = (SELECT MAX(CREDITS) FROM COURSE NATURAL JOIN DEPARTMENT WHERE TITLE='CS' GROUP BY DEPT_NAME HAVING COUNT(COURSE_ID)>2)
explanation: The only syntactic difference between Q1 and Q2 is the DISTINCT keyword that Q1 applies to the projection list.  Both queries first compute a single numeric value (call it MAX_C) with the nested sub-query.  They then return all rows from COURSE whose CREDITS equal MAX_C, but Q1 eliminates duplicate DEPT_NAMEs while Q2 keeps all of them.  Therefore the two queries return different results whenever at least two qualifying COURSE rows have the same DEPT_NAME – Q2 repeats that name, Q1 shows it once.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO DEPARTMENT (DEPT_NAME, BUILDING, BUDGET) VALUES
  (1, 10, 10000),
  (2, 20, 20000);

-- dept 1 has three CS courses (TITLE = 100) ; two of them share the same 5-credit value
INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES
  (1, 100, 1, 5),  -- CS course, 5 credits
  (2, 100, 1, 5),  -- another CS course, same dept & credits (causes duplicate)
  (3, 100, 1, 4),  -- CS course, 4 credits (gives dept 1 > 2 CS courses)
  (4, 200, 2, 5);  -- Non-CS course in dept 2, but has 5 credits, so it matches outer WHERE
counterexample_dsp: Make one department (dept 1) have >2 CS courses so that the sub-query yields exactly one row (its max credits = 5).  Provide two of those CS courses with the same credit 5, and add another course with credit 5 in a different department (dept 2).  The outer WHERE clause will match three rows; Q1 will output the list ‘1,2’, while Q2 will output ‘1,1,2’, revealing the difference caused by DISTINCT.

q1: SELECT STUDENT.ID, STUDENT.NAME FROM STUDENT JOIN (SELECT TAKES.ID, S.TIME_SLOT_ID, S.YEAR FROM TAKES JOIN SECTION AS S ON TAKES.COURSE_ID = S.COURSE_ID AND TAKES.SEC_ID = S.SEC_ID GROUP BY TAKES.ID, S.TIME_SLOT_ID, S.YEAR HAVING COUNT(S.TIME_SLOT_ID) > 1) AS A ON STUDENT.ID = A.ID GROUP BY STUDENT.ID, STUDENT.NAME HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT STUDENT.ID) > 2
q2: SELECT STUDENT.ID, STUDENT.NAME FROM STUDENT JOIN (SELECT TAKES.ID, S.TIME_SLOT_ID, S.YEAR FROM TAKES JOIN SECTION AS S ON TAKES.COURSE_ID = S.COURSE_ID AND TAKES.SEC_ID = S.SEC_ID GROUP BY TAKES.ID, S.TIME_SLOT_ID, S.YEAR HAVING SUM(S.TIME_SLOT_ID) > 1) AS A ON STUDENT.ID = A.ID GROUP BY STUDENT.ID, STUDENT.NAME HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT STUDENT.ID) > 2
explanation: The two queries differ only inside their inner sub-query A – one uses HAVING COUNT(…) > 1, the other HAVING SUM(…) > 1 – so A can indeed return different sets of (ID , TIME_SLOT_ID , YEAR) rows.  However this difference can never be observed, because the outer query groups again on STUDENT.ID and STUDENT.NAME and then keeps only those groups that satisfy HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT STUDENT.ID) > 2.  Since STUDENT.ID is part of the GROUP BY list, every group contains at most one distinct STUDENT.ID value (1 if the ID is NOT NULL, 0 if the ID is NULL), therefore the predicate COUNT(DISTINCT STUDENT.ID) > 2 can never be true.  Both Q1 and Q2 therefore return the empty result set for every possible database – they are logically equivalent and no counter-example exists.
counterexample: -- no INSERTs are necessary because the queries are equivalent for every database
counterexample_dsp: No data configuration can make the outer HAVING clause evaluate to TRUE, hence no counterexample is possible.  Any database content (even an empty one) will make both queries return the same (empty) result.

q1: SELECT SUM(T) AS SU FROM (SELECT YEAR AS T FROM TEACHES NATURAL JOIN INSTRUCTOR GROUP BY YEAR, COURSE_ID HAVING COUNT(ID)>4) AS TEMP GROUP BY T
q2: SELECT SUM(T) AS SU FROM (SELECT YEAR AS T FROM TEACHES NATURAL JOIN INSTRUCTOR GROUP BY YEAR HAVING COUNT(ID)>4) AS TEMP GROUP BY T
explanation:
Both queries look at the result of TEACHES NATURAL JOIN INSTRUCTOR.
• Q1 first groups BY (YEAR , COURSE_ID).  The HAVING condition COUNT(ID) > 4 is therefore applied per (year, course) pair.  Only years belonging to some course that has at least 5 instructors survive.  If no single course of a year reaches this threshold the year disappears completely from the result set.
• Q2 groups only BY YEAR.  Here all rows of the same year are pooled together before the HAVING test.  Consequently a year with many instructors spread over several different courses can pass the HAVING clause even if none of its individual courses would have passed in Q1.
Because the level of aggregation that the COUNT() is evaluated on is different (YEAR,COURSE_ID  vs  YEAR) the two queries disagree whenever the total number of instructors in a year is >4 but every single course inside that year has ≤4 instructors.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO INSTRUCTOR (ID, NAME, SALARY, DEPT_NAME) VALUES
  (1, 0, 0, 0),
  (2, 0, 0, 0),
  (3, 0, 0, 0),
  (4, 0, 0, 0),
  (5, 0, 0, 0),
  (6, 0, 0, 0);

-- course 101, 3 instructors in 2021
INSERT INTO TEACHES (ID, COURSE_ID, SEC_ID, YEAR, SEMESTER, INSTRUCTOR) VALUES
  (1, 101, 1, 2021, 1, 1),
  (2, 101, 2, 2021, 1, 2),
  (3, 101, 3, 2021, 1, 3);

-- course 102, another 3 instructors in the same year 2021
INSERT INTO TEACHES (ID, COURSE_ID, SEC_ID, YEAR, SEMESTER, INSTRUCTOR) VALUES
  (4, 102, 1, 2021, 1, 4),
  (5, 102, 2, 2021, 1, 5),
  (6, 102, 3, 2021, 1, 6);
counterexample_dsp:
Create one year (2021) with two different courses.  Each course is taught by exactly three distinct instructors (i.e. 6 instructors in total).  For that year:
• Per-course counts are 3 → they do NOT satisfy COUNT(ID) > 4 (Q1 rejects the year).
• Year total is 6 → it DOES satisfy COUNT(ID) > 4 (Q2 keeps the year).
No other data are needed, and no schema constraint is violated.

q1: SELECT COURSE_ID, TITLE FROM COURSE
q2: SELECT COURSE_ID, TITLE FROM COURSE WHERE CREDITS > 3
explanation: Q1 returns every row from COURSE, while Q2 adds a WHERE-condition that keeps only rows whose CREDITS value is strictly greater than 3. Any course whose CREDITS is NULL, 3 or less will therefore appear in Q1 but be filtered out of Q2, so the result sets can differ.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES (1, 100, 10, 3);
INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES (2, 200, 20, 4);
counterexample_dsp: Create at least one COURSE row whose CREDITS is ≤ 3 (or NULL). That row survives in Q1 but is eliminated by Q2’s CREDITS > 3 predicate. No schema constraint forbids such a value, so the difference is allowed.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT COURSE.COURSE_ID, COURSE.TITLE, TEACHES.ID FROM COURSE JOIN TEACHES WHERE COURSE.COURSE_ID = TEACHES.COURSE_ID AND TEACHES.YEAR = 2010
q2: SELECT DISTINCT COURSE.COURSE_ID, COURSE.TITLE, TEACHES.ID FROM COURSE JOIN TEACHES WHERE COURSE.COURSE_ID >= TEACHES.COURSE_ID AND TEACHES.YEAR = 2010
explanation: Q1 only keeps rows where COURSE.COURSE_ID equals TEACHES.COURSE_ID; Q2 keeps rows where the course id is *greater-than or equal* to the teaches course id. Whenever there is a COURSE record whose id is larger than (but not equal to) a TEACHES record from 2010, Q2 will produce extra joined rows, while Q1 will not. DISTINCT cannot eliminate this difference because the projected COURSE_ID values differ.
counterexample_dsp: Have one TEACHES row for course 1 in year 2010 and two COURSE rows (ids 1 and 2). Course 2 has no matching TEACHES row. With the >= predicate, course 2 still pairs with the teaches row for course 1, yielding an extra result that is absent from Q1.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT INSTRUCTOR.ID, INSTRUCTOR.NAME, TEACHES.COURSE_ID FROM INSTRUCTOR LEFT OUTER JOIN TEACHES ON INSTRUCTOR.ID > TEACHES.ID
q2: SELECT DISTINCT INSTRUCTOR.ID, INSTRUCTOR.NAME, TEACHES.COURSE_ID FROM INSTRUCTOR, TEACHES WHERE INSTRUCTOR.ID = TEACHES.ID
explanation:
Q1 keeps EVERY instructor (LEFT OUTER JOIN) and pairs an instructor with any TEACHES-rows whose TEACHES.ID is smaller (condition  INSTRUCTOR.ID > TEACHES.ID).  If no such TEACHES row exists the instructor is still kept, the TEACHES columns become NULL.  
Q2, in contrast, is an INNER join with an equality predicate (INSTRUCTOR.ID = TEACHES.ID); therefore it returns a row only when an instructor has a TEACHES row with the SAME id.  
Because the join predicate is different (>  vs =) and because Q1 is outer while Q2 is inner, the two queries can – and usually will – return different results.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO INSTRUCTOR (ID, NAME, SALARY, DEPT_NAME) VALUES (10, 1001, 50000, 1);
INSERT INTO TEACHES   (ID, COURSE_ID, SEC_ID, YEAR, SEMESTER, INSTRUCTOR) VALUES (5, 999, 1, 2023, 1, 10);
counterexample_dsp: Create one instructor whose id is bigger than the id that appears in a single TEACHES row.  The instructor therefore joins to that TEACHES row in Q1 (10 > 5), while Q2 finds no row (10 ≠ 5).  This satisfies all schema requirements and immediately shows the divergence.

q1: WITH S AS (SELECT ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR FROM TAKES NATURAL JOIN SECTION GROUP BY ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT TIME_SLOT_ID)>4) SELECT DISTINCT ID,NAME FROM S NATURAL JOIN STUDENT
q2: WITH S AS (SELECT ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR FROM TAKES NATURAL JOIN SECTION GROUP BY ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT TIME_SLOT_ID)>5) SELECT DISTINCT ID,NAME FROM S NATURAL JOIN STUDENT
explanation: The two queries are in fact logically equivalent for every possible database instance, hence they can never return different results.  Because TIME_SLOT_ID is included in the GROUP BY list, every group produced by the sub-query S contains rows with one (or zero, when TIME_SLOT_ID is NULL) single value of TIME_SLOT_ID. Consequently COUNT(DISTINCT TIME_SLOT_ID) can only be 0 or 1. The HAVING predicates (> 4 in Q1 and > 5 in Q2) are therefore always FALSE, so S is always empty and both Q1 and Q2 return the empty set. Since the result is necessarily the same (∅) for every database, no counter-example can exist.
counterexample: -- No INSERTs – the queries are equivalent for all databases
counterexample_dsp: No set of rows can make COUNT(DISTINCT TIME_SLOT_ID) equal to 5 in a group that already has TIME_SLOT_ID in its GROUP BY keys; therefore the condition for differing outputs is unachievable.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT DEPT_NAME FROM COURSE WHERE CREDITS=(SELECT MAX(CREDITS) FROM COURSE)
q2: SELECT DISTINCT DEPT_NAME FROM COURSE AS C JOIN (SELECT MAX(CREDITS) AS MAX_CREDITS FROM COURSE GROUP BY DEPT_NAME) AS A WHERE C.CREDITS = A.MAX_CREDITS
explanation: Q1 finds departments that own a course whose number of credits equals the single highest credit value that exists in the whole COURSE table. Q2 first computes every department’s local maximum credit value, then (because of a CROSS-JOIN without an ON-clause) keeps every course whose credit equals *any* of those local maxima. Hence Q2 returns departments whose maximum can be lower than the global maximum, so the two queries differ whenever at least one department’s local-max credit is smaller than the global maximum.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES
  (1, 111, 10, 5),  -- global-max course (dept 10)
  (2, 112, 10, 3),  -- another course in dept 10
  (3, 211, 20, 4);  -- local-max course in dept 20 (below global max)
counterexample_dsp: Have two departments.  Dept 10 has a 5-credit course (the global maximum) plus another course.  Dept 20’s most demanding course is 4 credits. 4 is a local maximum for dept 20 but not the global maximum.  Q1 therefore returns only dept 10, while Q2 returns dept 10 and dept 20.
